nuance.usage_note: Americans use speed dial for saved numbers on cell phones and landlines, often for family or doctors. People sometimes say 'Put me on speed dial' to mean 'I want you to be easy to reach.' Smartphones often call this favorites, so a casual listener may understand either word.

distinctions.note: Contacts is the whole phone address book, while speed dial is a shortcut for a few important numbers.
Favorites is the common smartphone term, while speed dial is older phone wording.

examples.everyday: Put your son's number on speed dial so you can reach him fast.
examples.professional: Can you add the support line to speed dial before the conference call?
examples.analytical: Speed dial reveals how older phones structured trust by placing a few relationships one touch away.

nuance.analogy: Speed dial is like a row of shortcut keys on a keyboard: one press takes you directly to the place you use most.
nuance.etymology: Speed from Old English spēd, 'success, prosperity'; dial from Latin dies, 'day', via the sundial.
common_mistakes: Saying speed dial as a verb; you usually say call a number on speed dial.
Saying put in speed dial; the usual phrase is put on speed dial.

conversation.text: My mom is still on my speed dial.
I have the pizza place on speed dial.
She has her lawyer on speed dial.

senses.definition: One who uses a sponge.
senses.example: The bather, a dedicated sponger, scrubbed the tub with a natural sea sponge every Saturday.

senses.definition: A parasitic hanger-on.
senses.example: My cousin is a sponger who never pays for dinner but always has a story.

senses.definition: A person or vessel employed in gathering sponges from the sea.
senses.example: The Greek sponger returned to Tarpon Springs with a boat full of sea sponges.

senses.definition: A device for sponging cloth by means of a perforated adjustable cylinder.
senses.example: The tailor fed the wool through the sponger to shrink it before cutting the suit.

core.definition: A person who lives off other people's money, food or hospitality and does not contribute anything in return.

pronunciation.tip: Sponge has one syllable with the short uh vowel, as in fun, not an oh sound. The ending is a rhotic reduced syllable, so the r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a sponger is an insult that suggests laziness and taking advantage of others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sponger in casual conversation about roommates, relatives or friends who always ask for money or meals. It can sound harsh, so use it carefully, especially with family. Close informal alternatives are freeloader and mooch.

distinctions.note: Freeloader is a very common American word for someone who gets free benefits, while sponger suggests a more persistent drain on others.
Mooch is a more casual word for asking others for things, often food or small amounts of money.

examples.everyday: My roommate is a total sponger, he never buys groceries and always eats my food.
examples.professional: I shouldn't have to tolerate a sponger on the project team who never reviews code.
examples.analytical: Nineteenth-century moralists often portrayed the idle aristocrat as a sponger who lived off the labor of tenants.

nuance.analogy: Like a sponge that soaks up water and never wrings out, the sponger takes in more than they give.
nuance.etymology: From sponge plus -er; the sense of freeloader comes from the verb to sponge, meaning to live at others' expense.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing sponge with an oh vowel, as in SPOHN-jer.
Using sponger as a neutral word; it is an insult and can offend people if used casually.

senses.definition: Exceptionally clean.
senses.example: spotless shirt

senses.definition: Impeccable and free from blemish.
senses.example: spotless nature

senses.definition: Lacking spots; unspotted.
senses.example: She kept the kitchen spotless, wiping every counter and mirror before guests arrived.

core.definition: Completely clean, with no dirt, stains, or marks anywhere.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SPOT. The final -less is a reduced 'lus' with a weak vowel, not a full 'less,' and the t is clear before the l.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spotless to praise a clean kitchen, car, or record. It can be used casually ('The bathroom is spotless!') or in formal writing. For a reputation, 'spotless record' is common and admiring.

distinctions.note: Clean is the general word; spotless is stronger and means without even a small mark anywhere.
Immaculate is more formal and can describe appearance or dress as well as cleanliness.

examples.everyday: Come on in, the house is spotless because my mom visited this morning.
examples.professional: The auditor found the financial records spotless, with every entry reconciled.
examples.analytical: The argument is not spotless; its premises carry assumptions that the author never defends.

nuance.analogy: Like a freshly polished window that shows nothing but the view, it has no smudge on it.
nuance.etymology: From spot (a mark) plus the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, 'spot-LESS,' which is unnatural.
Using spotless for 'clean' in a weak sense; it implies absolutely no marks.

conversation.text: She cleaned the kitchen until it was spotless.
The hotel room was spotless when we checked in.
Leave the apartment spotless if you want your deposit back.

senses.definition: The property of being spotless.

core.definition: The quality of being completely clean and free from any stain, mark, or blemish.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the middle '-less' to a schwa so it sounds like 'lus'. The ending '-ness' is a short, unstressed 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises cleanliness, purity, or a reputation free of any stain, but it can sound overly formal in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spotlessness mainly in writing and in formal or descriptive speech, such as reviews, reports, or literary descriptions. In everyday conversation, people usually say 'how clean it is' or 'the cleanliness'. The word can also be used figuratively for a reputation or character without stain.

distinctions.note: Cleanliness is the general, everyday word for the state of being clean. Spotlessness is stronger and implies a complete absence of any mark or stain.
Purity can be physical, moral, or chemical, and is broader. Spotlessness emphasizes the absence of visible marks or stains, although it can be used figuratively.

examples.everyday: I was impressed by the spotlessness of their bathroom when we visited last weekend.
examples.professional: The auditor praised the spotlessness of the warehouse inventory records, which had no discrepancies.
examples.analytical: Her reputation for moral spotlessness made the accusation seem absurd to her colleagues, though it also made any mistake look more serious.

nuance.analogy: Spotlessness is like a white sheet of paper with no marks on it, where every mark would be immediately visible.
nuance.etymology: From spotless (spot plus -less) and the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'liss' instead of a reduced 'lus'.
Using spotlessness in casual speech where cleanliness is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament, the Greek word aspilos means 'unstained' or 'without spot', and it describes the purity expected of Christ and of the church. Ephesians 5:27 speaks of the church being presented without spot or wrinkle, which describes the holiness Christ intends for his people. 1 Peter 1:19 compares Christ to an unblemished, spotless lamb, linking his redemption to sacrificial purity.

senses.definition: To weaken, as a joint, ligament, or muscle, by sudden and excessive exertion, as by wrenching; to overstrain, or stretch injuriously, but without luxation.
senses.example: He sprained his knee after falling off the bicycle.

senses.definition: The act or result of spraining; lameness caused by spraining.
senses.example: a bad sprain of the wrist

core.definition: To injure a joint or ligament by twisting or stretching it suddenly and too far.

pronunciation.tip: The r is pronounced clearly and blends into the consonant cluster, so the word is one syllable. Keep the vowel as a long 'ay' diphthong with the final n clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sprain for a common injury from a fall, a misstep, or sports, and people often say 'I sprained my ankle' in everyday talk. It is also used as a noun, 'a bad sprain.' Doctors may advise RICE: rest, ice, compression, and elevation.

distinctions.note: A strain stretches a muscle or tendon, while a sprain injures a ligament that connects bones at a joint.
Twist is a general motion; sprain is the injury that can result from a twist.

examples.everyday: I sprained my wrist trying to catch the frisbee at the park.
examples.professional: Please report any injury, including a sprain, to the safety office so we can log it properly.
examples.analytical: A sprain differs from a strain in the tissue involved, which determines the expected recovery time.

nuance.analogy: Like a rope pulled too hard that frays at its knot, the ligament is overstretched at the joint.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly from Old French espreindre, 'to press out.'
common_mistakes: Confusing sprain with strain, which affects different tissues.
Using 'sprained' as a verb in the past without the -ed ending, saying 'I sprain my ankle yesterday.'

conversation.text: It's not broken; it's just a sprain.
I sprained my wrist playing basketball.
A bad sprain can take a few weeks to heal.

senses.definition: A systematic cleaning of a residence at the end of winter.
A systematic cleaning, reorganization, or weeding out of a system.
senses.example: Every April we do spring cleaning, purging old files from the shared drive.

core.definition: A thorough cleaning of a home, often done in late winter or early spring, including washing windows, carpets, and closets.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'clean' in 'CLEAN-ing,' and 'spring' gets secondary stress. The r in 'spring' is clear, and the 'ing' ending is a light, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive and wholesome. It suggests fresh starts and seasonal renewal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase for a big, once-a-year deep clean, often before guests arrive or as a fresh start after winter. It can also be used figuratively for cleaning out files, email, or a messy process at work. A natural reply to someone saying they are doing it is 'Good for you!' or 'Nice, that is a big job.'

distinctions.note: Tidying up is a quick putting-away of items, while spring cleaning is a deep, thorough cleaning of the whole house.
Decluttering focuses on removing unneeded items, while spring cleaning usually includes both removing and scrubbing.

examples.everyday: We are doing spring cleaning this weekend, so the garage is going to be a mess for a while.
examples.professional: Our team is doing spring cleaning on the shared drive, archiving old project folders and deleting duplicates.
examples.analytical: Spring cleaning can be read as a ritual that marks the passage from winter's enclosure to the openness of the new season.

nuance.analogy: Spring cleaning is like a reset button for a home, clearing away the dust that built up while the windows stayed shut.
nuance.etymology: Spring refers to the season, and cleaning is from Old English 'clænsian,' meaning to make clean.
common_mistakes: Saying 'spring clean' as a verb without 'do'; Americans say 'do spring cleaning' or 'we are cleaning.'
Pronouncing the stress evenly on both words; the 'clean' syllable is stronger.

conversation.text: We do spring cleaning every April and wash all the windows.
It's time for some spring cleaning; the garage is a disaster.
I found my old guitar during spring cleaning.

senses.definition: An actor on the stage.
One who stages a theatrical performance.
senses.example: The stager rehearsed each scene with the actors until the timing felt natural.

senses.definition: One who has long acted on the stage of life; a practitioner; a person of experience, or of skill derived from long experience.
A horse used in drawing a stagecoach.

core.definition: An experienced person who has worked for a long time in a field or public life, often used in the phrase old stager.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -er is a weak, r-colored vowel, not a long ee sound, so do not say STAY-jee.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral: it praises long experience, sometimes with a hint of age or ironic affection.
nuance.usage_note: Stager is rare in modern American speech; you mainly meet it in the phrase old stager, in journalism, memoirs, or literary writing about politics or the arts. Most Americans would say veteran or old hand instead. Use it sparingly and only when you want a slightly formal flavor.

distinctions.note: Veteran is the everyday word for someone with long experience; stager is more literary and often suggests experience in public or performance settings.
Old hand is more colloquial and practical; old stager carries a more formal and slightly ironic air.

examples.everyday: Ask Dan about the old neighborhood; he's an old stager and knows everyone.
examples.professional: Our CFO is an old stager who has seen three recessions and knows which numbers to trust.
examples.analytical: The historian describes the senator as an old stager whose long career gave him a feel for the rhythms of political life.

nuance.analogy: Like a path worn smooth by many feet, a stager has walked the same route so often that it has become second nature.
nuance.etymology: From stage with the agent suffix -er; the figurative sense of an experienced veteran extends the idea of long performance.
common_mistakes: Using stager as a common word for an actor; actor is the normal term, and stager is rare and literary.
Saying STAY-jee; the ending is a weak, r-colored vowel.

senses.definition: An adult male horse.
Specifically, one that is uncastrated.
A male horse kept primarily as a stud.
A very virile and sexually-inclined man or (rarely) woman.

core.definition: An adult male horse, especially one that is not castrated and is kept for breeding.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and treat -lion as one unstressed syllable that sounds like 'yun'. It has two syllables, not three.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in horse talk. As a metaphor for a man it can be playful or objectifying, so use it carefully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stallion mainly in ranching, horse breeding and racing. In everyday talk most people say horse or male horse. Calling a man a stallion is a playful or sometimes crude compliment, so avoid it at work.

distinctions.note: A gelding is a castrated male horse, while a stallion is an uncastrated adult male.
A mare is an adult female horse, while a stallion is an adult male.

examples.everyday: The farm down the road keeps a big stallion that everyone stops to see.
examples.professional: Our breeding program needs a stallion with a proven record for calm temperament.
examples.analytical: The stallion in the old myth stands for untamed strength that the rider must learn to direct.

nuance.analogy: Like a thoroughbred in a stable, powerful and hard to handle until it is trained.
nuance.etymology: From Old French estalon, meaning a stud horse.
common_mistakes: Using stallion for any male horse; a castrated male is called a gelding.
Pronouncing it as three syllables, like 'stal-ee-on'; it has two.

stallion.etymology: From Middle English *stalion*, from Middle French *estalon* (whence modern French *étalon*), of origin, akin to *stall*.

senses.definition: Firmly or solidly built.
senses.example: The stalwart oak door was built to withstand any storm.

senses.definition: Courageous.
senses.example: The stalwart firefighter ran back into the burning house to find the child.

senses.definition: Determined; staunch.
senses.example: Even after losing three elections, he remained stalwart in his commitment to reform.

senses.definition: One who has a strong build.
senses.example: The stalwart was a big man who had played linebacker in college.

senses.definition: One who firmly supports a cause.
senses.example: She was a stalwart of the local party, volunteering every election season for decades.

senses.definition: One who is dependable.
senses.example: The party's staunchest stalwarts constitute the President's redoubtable bulwark against the latter bribery accusations.

core.definition: Loyal, dependable and strongly committed to a person, group or cause.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final 'ar' is reduced to a quiet 'er', so the word has two syllables after the stress, not three.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting reliability and courage. It praises people who stay steady under pressure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stalwart' mainly in news, speeches and writing about political or community supporters, such as 'a stalwart supporter of the team.' In casual speech, people more often say 'loyal' or 'solid.' It works best as praise and is rarely used for objects.

distinctions.note: Loyal is common and general, while stalwart adds a sense of firmness and steadiness in difficult times.
Staunch is very close in meaning and appears in similar contexts, but it is spelled differently in the sense of 'firm' and is often used with supporters or allies.

examples.everyday: My grandmother has been a stalwart member of our church choir for forty years.
examples.professional: She has been a stalwart advocate for our customers during every product rollout.
examples.analytical: The reformers were stalwart in their commitment, yet their stalwart resistance to compromise limited their influence.

nuance.analogy: A stalwart supporter is like an old oak tree that stays standing through every storm.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'stalworth,' meaning strong, brave or fit for service.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'stall-wart' with a strong final syllable.
Using 'stalwart' for a physical object as if it meant only 'sturdy', when it usually describes people.

stalwart.etymology: Borrowed from Scots *stalwart* under the influence of Walter Scott, displacing earlier, wherewith it forms a doublet.

senses.definition: To begin.
senses.example: She started off with a lullaby.

senses.definition: To set out on a trip.
senses.example: They started off on horseback.

senses.definition: To instigate someone to laugh or cry or to begin talking about something they often talk about.
senses.example: Don't start him off about that again.

core.definition: To begin, especially a process, journey or activity, often in a particular way or with a first step.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on OFF, with lighter stress on START. Keep the t crisp, because it comes before a stressed vowel and should not soften into a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly. It is practical and used for ordinary beginnings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use start off for beginning a project, meeting or day, often in the phrases 'start off with' or 'start off on the right foot'. For setting out on a trip, people more often say 'head out' or 'take off'. It is common in both speech and writing.

distinctions.note: 'Start off' stresses the first stage or a specific way of beginning, as in 'start off well'; 'start' alone is the general verb.
'Start out' often describes beginning in a certain condition or role, as in 'start out as an intern'; 'start off' more often refers to the first action or stage of an event.

collocations: start off on the right foot

examples.everyday: Let's start off with some chips and salsa while we wait for the pizza.
examples.professional: I'd like to start off the call by reviewing the pilot results before we discuss next steps.
examples.analytical: The argument starts off by assuming free will, and that assumption shapes every conclusion that follows.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay race: the first runner starts the baton moving, and every later step depends on that first handoff.
nuance.etymology: From start (Old English styrtan, to leap) plus off.
common_mistakes: Writing 'start off to do' in formal English; Americans prefer 'start off by doing' or 'start off with' a noun.
Mixing up 'start off' and 'start out'; both mean begin, but 'start out' often describes your original condition or role.

senses.definition: In contact, or in communication.
senses.example: Let's stay in touch.

senses.definition: Outside the playing area or touching the touchlines of the playing area.
senses.example: Kick the ball in touch.

core.definition: To keep communicating with someone over time, for example by phone, text, email or social media, after you are no longer in regular contact.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TOUCH, the final content word. In a phrase, in is reduced to a quick ihn, so say stay-in-TUCH as if it were one smooth unit.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests friendliness and continued interest in someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say stay in touch when parting from friends, coworkers or classmates, often as a polite goodbye. A natural reply is Definitely, I will, or Sounds good, let's stay in touch. When naming the person, use stay in touch with, as in I stay in touch with my college roommate.

distinctions.note: Keep in touch and stay in touch are almost identical; stay in touch is slightly more common in American speech.
Get in touch means to make first contact, while stay in touch means to maintain existing contact over time.

collocations: stay in touch over the phone
stay in touch during the trip

examples.everyday: It was great meeting you at the barbecue, so let's stay in touch and get coffee next month.
examples.professional: Thanks for the call, and please stay in touch with me about the rollout schedule through the end of the quarter.
examples.analytical: Scholars who stay in touch across disciplines often produce work that bridges fields and resists narrow specialization.

nuance.analogy: Staying in touch is like keeping a thread running between two spools: the connection stays alive even when the two ends are far apart.
common_mistakes: Omitting with when naming the person, as in I stay in touch my friend instead of I stay in touch with my friend.
Using in touch alone for a first contact, when get in touch is the natural phrase.

conversation.text: Let's stay in touch. Here's my number.
It's hard to stay in touch with college friends when everyone has kids.
We've stayed in touch for twenty years, mostly through Christmas cards.

senses.definition: One who steals; a thief.
senses.example: a child-stealer

senses.definition: The endmost plank of a strake which stops short of the stem or stern.
senses.example: The shipwright fitted a stealer at the stern, where the strake stopped short of the post.

senses.definition: Clipping of infostealer.
senses.example: The security team found a stealer hidden in the attachment, copying saved browser passwords.

core.definition: A person who takes someone else's property without permission; a thief.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, STEEL. The final -er is a weak, r-colored syllable, so do not say STEEL-ah as in some British speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a person who takes things illegally or secretly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always say 'thief' or 'robber' in everyday talk, so 'stealer' sounds unusual or literary. The word now appears mainly in compounds such as 'scene stealer' and in computing terms like 'infostealer' or 'password stealer', which refer to malicious software.

distinctions.note: Thief is the everyday, common word for someone who steals, while stealer is rare and more literary.
A robber takes property by force or threat, while a stealer takes it secretly or without permission.
A pickpocket specifically steals from people's pockets or bags in public, while stealer is a general term.

examples.everyday: Our dog is the cookie stealer in this house, so keep the counter clear.
examples.professional: The security team flagged a password stealer hidden in an email attachment and blocked it before anyone opened it.
examples.analytical: Medieval moral writers often portrayed the stealer as a figure who broke both the law and the trust that holds a community together.

nuance.analogy: A stealer is like a thief in a costume: the meaning is clear, but everyday Americans would simply say thief.
nuance.etymology: From the verb steal (Old English stelan) with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using 'stealer' in ordinary conversation where 'thief' is the natural word.
Confusing 'stealer' with 'stealthy', which means sneaky or secret, not a person who steals.

senses.definition: A course followed by a person in walking or as walking.
senses.example: She followed the steps of the girl beside her

senses.definition: A flight of stairs, especially out of doors.
senses.example: He clumped up the steps.

core.definition: A set of stairs, especially outdoors, that leads up to a door, porch or building.

pronunciation.tip: The word ends in a consonant cluster, ps, so pronounce the p and then the s with no extra vowel. The vowel is short e, as in step.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a physical feature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'front steps' or 'porch steps' for stairs outside a house. Inside a building they usually say 'stairs' or 'staircase.' Steps can also mean actions taken toward a goal, as in 'take steps to fix the problem,' which is a different and very common meaning.

distinctions.note: Stairs is used for stairs inside or outside; steps is especially common for short outdoor flights, such as those to a porch.
Stairway is the structure that contains stairs, often indoors; steps are the individual stair units or the set itself outdoors.

examples.everyday: Please don't leave your bike on the front steps, because my dad keeps tripping over it.
examples.professional: The building's entrance has concrete steps, so the contractor will need to build a ramp for the delivery.
examples.analytical: Ancient temples often ascended steps that marked a movement from the ordinary to the sacred, making the climb itself a form of worship.

nuance.analogy: Like a ladder built into the side of a hill, letting you climb one level at a time.
nuance.etymology: From Old English stæpe (step or stair), the plural form of step.
common_mistakes: Using steps for indoor stairs; Americans usually say stairs for the staircase in a house.
Confusing steps meaning stairs with steps meaning actions; take steps means act to achieve something.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the idea of a step or stair is ma'alah, from a root meaning to go up or ascend; the Psalms of Ascent (Psalms 120 to 134) use the related word ma'alot. Psalm 37:23 says that a person's steps are directed by the LORD, meaning God guides the course of a life. Psalm 40:2 describes God lifting the psalmist from a pit and setting his feet on a rock so that his steps are made firm. Both passages use steps to describe the course of a human life under God's care.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to or characteristic of a stereotype; stereotypical.
senses.example: The child's stereotypic hand-flapping during excitement prompted the pediatrician to ask further questions.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to or characteristic of a stereotypy.
senses.example: The child's stereotypic hand-flapping during excitement prompted the pediatrician to ask further questions.

core.definition: Conforming to a stereotype; typical, predictable or oversimplified in the way a group or behavior is portrayed.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the -TYP- syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, so don't give each vowel full value.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on context. In psychology and neurology it is descriptive; in social commentary it is critical.
nuance.usage_note: Stereotypic is less common in American speech than stereotypical, and most Americans would use stereotypical for a social stereotype. Stereotypic appears more often in technical writing about repetitive behavior, where it describes stereotypy. In everyday talk, choose stereotypical.

distinctions.note: The two are close in meaning, but stereotypical is the everyday choice for social stereotypes, while stereotypic is rarer and more technical.
Stereotyped often describes something repeated without originality; stereotypic describes something that matches a type or a repetitive pattern.

examples.everyday: My friend says his dog's pacing is a stereotypic habit, but the vet isn't worried.
examples.professional: The team's report flagged stereotypic movements in the test subjects that needed closer review.
examples.analytical: Scholars distinguish stereotypic patterns of behavior from the social stereotypes that shape how those patterns are interpreted.

nuance.analogy: Like a mold that makes every cast come out identical; the shape repeats whatever the material.
nuance.etymology: From stereotype, from Greek stereos ('solid, firm') and typos ('impression'), plus the adjective suffix -ic.
common_mistakes: Using stereotypic in everyday conversation where stereotypical is the natural word.
Misplacing the stress on the first syllable instead of the -TYP- syllable.

senses.definition: A woman who works at housekeeping and passenger service aboard a ship, yacht, or other type of boat that carries passengers.
senses.example: On the ferry, the stewardess handed each passenger a warm towel before we reached the island.

senses.definition: A female steward (any sense).
senses.example: Our stewardess on the cruise ship, Maria, remembered every passenger's name by the second day.

senses.definition: (dated) A female flight attendant (a member of the crew of an airplane who is responsible for the comfort and safety of its passengers).
senses.label: dated

core.definition: (dated) A woman who works as a crew member on an airplane, serving passengers and helping ensure their safety and comfort; now usually called a flight attendant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a weak, rhotic 'er' that Americans often reduce almost to nothing. The final '-ess' is unstressed and sounds like 'iss'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to dated; it can sound old-fashioned or gendered, so most Americans now say flight attendant.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, flight attendant has been the standard job title for decades, and airlines dropped stewardess in the 1970s because it was gendered. You will still hear older people use it or see it in films and memoirs. Ship and boat stewardesses are a much rarer meaning and are not used in everyday American speech.

distinctions.note: Flight attendant is the current, gender-neutral term used by American airlines and in everyday speech.
Steward is the gender-neutral term for a male or unspecified crew member who serves passengers; stewardess specifies a woman and is dated.

examples.everyday: My aunt worked as a stewardess for Pan Am back in the seventies, and she still has her old wings pin.
examples.professional: Our HR policy uses flight attendant rather than stewardess in all job postings and internal documents.
examples.analytical: The word stewardess encoded a mid-century assumption that caring for passengers was women's work, which is why the industry moved to gender-neutral terms.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a mail carrier a mailman: the job is the same, but the older word carries an outdated picture of who does it.
nuance.etymology: From steward, from Old English stigweard, 'hall keeper', with the feminine suffix -ess.
common_mistakes: Using stewardess for a current American flight crew member, which many people will hear as outdated.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: Synonym of evergreen.

core.definition: Always green; keeping its leaves through the year, like an evergreen plant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls mainly on GREEN, with 'still' slightly lighter. Say the r in 'green' clearly, since American speech is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to poetic, suggesting lasting freshness through all seasons.
nuance.usage_note: This word is rare in modern American English. You'll find it in older poetry or nature writing. Americans say 'evergreen' for plants such as pines, firs, and hollies, so use that word in everyday speech; 'still-green' sounds archaic or literary.

distinctions.note: Evergreen is the common everyday term for plants that keep their foliage; still-green is an archaic or poetic synonym.
Green alone describes a color; still-green adds the idea of staying green through every season.

examples.everyday: Grandpa used to call those pines still-green, which sounded old-fashioned to us kids.
examples.professional: Our nursery catalog lists the holly as evergreen, although some older customers still ask for still-green varieties.
examples.analytical: Romantic poets often used still-green imagery to set eternal life against the cycle of decay.

nuance.analogy: Like a stage set of spring that is never packed away.
nuance.etymology: From still, meaning always or ever, plus green.
common_mistakes: Using still-green in ordinary conversation where Americans say evergreen.
Putting the main stress on still instead of on the color word green.

senses.definition: Stiffly, or in an unnatural manner.

core.definition: In a stiff, unnatural, or overly formal way that lacks ease and flow.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is short and reduced, and the final -ly is a light 'lee' that should not be stretched.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests awkwardness and a lack of natural ease.
nuance.usage_note: This word is rare in spoken American English. You'll see it in reviews of writing or acting, or in describing a speaker who reads prepared lines too formally. Americans more often say 'awkwardly', 'stiffly', or 'in a stilted way'. Use it for speech, writing, or performance rather than for ordinary body movement.

distinctions.note: Stiffly describes physical rigidity; stiltedly describes speech or writing that sounds forced and unnatural.
Awkwardly is a broad term for clumsiness; stiltedly is narrower, referring to formal or unnatural expression.

examples.professional: The product copy reads stiltedly, so we should rewrite it in a plain, friendly voice for customers.
examples.analytical: The translation renders Paul's rhetoric stiltedly, flattening a vivid argument into formal and lifeless prose.

nuance.analogy: Like a dancer counting every step out loud: each move is correct, but nothing flows.
nuance.etymology: From stilted, the adjective from stilt, with the adverbial ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using it for physical movement; say 'stiffly' for stiff body motion.
Stressing the second syllable as stil-TID-lee; the stress falls on the first syllable.

senses.definition: A pair of metal tongs with heated ceramic plates used for straightening hair.
Anyone or anything which straightens.
A prearranged fight to settle a dispute.
A bribe.

core.definition: A tool with heated metal plates that you clamp onto hair to make it straight; also a person or thing that straightens things out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, STRAYT, and the middle syllable is weak, often dropped, so it sounds like two syllables. Keep the American r clear at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a practical tool, so it fits any setting and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for the hair tool all the time, in drugstores, salons and everyday talk. You may also hear 'flat iron', which is especially common in salons and beauty product listings. In casual talk you might ask 'Can I borrow your straightener?' and a natural reply is 'Sure, it's in the bathroom drawer.' The old sense of a prearranged fight is rare today.

distinctions.note: In American salons and beauty talk the two words usually name the same hair tool; 'flat iron' is especially common in salons and product descriptions.
A curling iron has a rounded barrel that curls hair, while a straightener has two flat plates that press hair straight.

collocations: heat protectant before using a straightener

examples.everyday: Can I borrow your straightener? My hair is totally frizzy today.
examples.professional: The salon's inventory list shows two straighteners on backorder, so please check stock before the Saturday rush.
examples.analytical: Straightener is a telling example of how one word can name a heated tool, a person who straightens things out, and an old prearranged fight.

nuance.analogy: A straightener works like an iron on a wrinkled shirt, pressing curly material flat.
nuance.etymology: From straighten (verb), from straight, from Old English strǣht, a past participle meaning 'stretched'.
common_mistakes: Using 'straighter', the comparative adjective, instead of the noun 'straightener'.
Dropping the stress or the r: say STRAYT-nur, not stray-TNUR or 'strate-nah'.

senses.definition: Hereditary character, quality, tendency, or disposition.
senses.example: There is a strain of madness in her family.

senses.definition: Language that is eloquent, poetic, or otherwise heightened.
senses.example: (The addition of quotations indicative of this usage is being sought:)

senses.definition: The act of straining, or the state of being strained.
senses.example: The strain of the long shift left the nurse exhausted by midnight.

senses.definition: A violent effort; an excessive and hurtful exertion or tension, as of the muscles.
senses.example: he jumped up with a strain

senses.definition: An injury resulting from violent effort; a sprain.
senses.example: He suffered a hamstring strain during Tuesday's run and missed practice.

senses.definition: A dimensionless measure of object deformation either referring to engineering strain or true strain.
senses.example: Engineers measured the bridge's strain under heavy loads using a digital sensor.

senses.definition: A particular variety of a microbe, virus, or other organism, usually a taxonomically infraspecific one.
senses.example: They say this year's flu virus is a particularly virulent strain.

senses.definition: Any sustained note or movement; a song; a distinct portion of an ode or other poem; also, the pervading note, or burden, of a song, poem, etc.
senses.example: The poet's final strain lingered in the air long after the choir fell silent.

senses.definition: (rare) A kind or sort (of person etc.).
senses.example: She came from a proud strain of farmers who never gave up.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To apply a force or forces to by stretching out.
senses.example: to strain a rope; to strain the shrouds of a ship

senses.definition: To damage by drawing, stretching, or the exertion of force.
senses.example: The gale strained the timbers of the ship.

senses.definition: To act upon, in any way, so as to cause change of form or volume, as when bending a beam.
senses.example: Heavy snow began to strain the old barn's roof beams over the winter.

senses.definition: To exert or struggle (to do something), especially to stretch (one's senses, faculties etc.) beyond what is normal or comfortable.
senses.example: Sitting in back, I strained to hear the speaker.

senses.definition: To stretch beyond its proper limit; to do violence to, in terms of intent or meaning.
senses.example: to strain the law in order to convict an accused person

senses.definition: To separate solid from liquid by passing through a strainer or colander.
senses.example: Strain the cooked pasta through a colander before adding the sauce.

senses.definition: To percolate; to be filtered.
senses.example: water straining through a sandy soil

senses.definition: To make uneasy or unnatural; to produce with apparent effort; to force; to constrain.
senses.example: He strained a smile during the awkward meeting, clearly uncomfortable with the news.

senses.definition: To urge with importunity; to press.
senses.example: to strain a petition or invitation

senses.definition: To make great demands on something.
senses.example: a story that strains credulity

senses.definition: To hug somebody; to hold somebody tightly.
senses.example: After months apart, she strained her son to her chest in a long hug.

core.definition: Physical or mental pressure or stress, or an injury from overusing or stretching a part of the body.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the long a of 'stay' and a firm n at the end. The r comes right after the t sound in str-, so keep the tongue back and avoid adding a vowel: 'strain', not 'suh-train'.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, meaning stress or injury. It is neutral in technical or biological contexts, such as a strain of virus.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use strain for a pulled muscle, as in 'I got a back strain', and for emotional or financial pressure, as in 'The budget is under strain.' Saying 'I'm under a lot of strain' is natural at work, and a common reply is 'Let's take a break.' The noun also means a variety of a virus, plant or bacterium, which is common in medical and science news.

distinctions.note: Stress is mostly mental or emotional pressure, while strain can also mean physical overexertion or injury, as in a muscle strain.
A sprain is an injury to a ligament at a joint, while a strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon.

examples.everyday: I got a back strain from lifting the boxes, so I'm taking it easy this weekend.
examples.professional: The long release cycle is putting a strain on the team, so we need to rebalance the workload.
examples.analytical: The debate reveals a strain between divine sovereignty and human responsibility that thinkers have long recognized.

nuance.analogy: Like a rope pulled too tight, strain is the pressure that stretches something until it weakens.
nuance.etymology: From Old French estreindre, from Latin stringere 'to draw tight'.
common_mistakes: Confusing strain, meaning stress or injury to a muscle, with sprain, which is an injury to a ligament.
Using 'strain' for a cold or illness; say 'a strain of flu' or 'a bad cold'.

strain.etymology: From Middle English *streen*, *strene*, *streon*, *istreon* (“race, stock, generation”), from Old English *strēon*, *ġestrēon* (“gain, wealth”), from **streun*, from Proto-Germanic **streuną* (“heap, treasure, profit, gain”), from Proto-Indo-European…

senses.definition: A person whom one does not know; a person who is neither a friend nor an acquaintance.
senses.example: That gentleman is a stranger to me.

senses.definition: An outsider or foreigner.
senses.example: When we visited Lisbon, I felt like a stranger who didn't speak a word of Portuguese.

senses.definition: One not admitted to communion or fellowship.
senses.example: The bishop's letter said that the excommunicated man was a stranger to the sacraments until he repented.

senses.definition: A newcomer.
senses.example: Our new neighbor is a stranger to the block, but she already knows everyone's name.

senses.definition: Used ironically to refer to a person who the speaker knows.
senses.example: Hello, stranger!

senses.definition: One not privy or party to an act, contract, or title; a mere intruder or intermeddler; one who interferes without right.
senses.example: Actual possession of land gives a good title against a stranger having no title.

senses.definition: A moth, Lacanobia blenna.
senses.example: The entomologist identified a stranger moth, Lacanobia blenna, attracted to our porch light.

core.definition: A person you do not know, someone who is neither a friend nor an acquaintance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-er' is an r-colored reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'ur' and doesn't need a separate hard 'g' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, though it can carry a note of caution in phrases like 'don't talk to strangers' and a warm note in 'treat strangers with kindness'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stranger' for a person you have never met, as in 'a complete stranger'. Parents often tell children not to talk to strangers. 'I'm a stranger here' is a natural way to say you are new to a place. 'Stranger danger' is a common informal phrase warning children about unknown adults.

distinctions.note: A foreigner is someone from another country, while a stranger is anyone you do not know, regardless of nationality.
An acquaintance is someone you know slightly, while a stranger is someone you have never met or know nothing about.

examples.everyday: A complete stranger helped me jump-start my car in the grocery store parking lot.
examples.professional: Our onboarding program pairs new hires with a buddy, so no one feels like a stranger on the first day.
examples.analytical: The parable asks who counts as a neighbor, suggesting that the stranger on the road is the one we must love.

nuance.analogy: A stranger is like an unread book on a shelf: you know it exists, but you have not yet learned what it says.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'estrangier', from Latin 'extraneus', meaning foreign or outside.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'stranger' with 'strange': 'a stranger' is a person, while 'strange' describes something odd.
Saying 'I'm stranger here' instead of 'I'm a stranger here'; the article 'a' is needed.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, the stranger is often the Hebrew ger, a resident alien living among Israel who needed protection and fair treatment, and the Greek xenos, a guest or foreigner. Lev 19:34 tells Israel to treat the resident stranger as one of their own. Heb 13:2 urges hospitality to strangers, noting that some have unknowingly entertained angels. Eph 2:19 says that Gentile believers are no longer strangers but fellow citizens with the saints.

senses.definition: A long, narrow flag, or piece of material used or seen as a decoration.
Strips of paper or other material used as confetti.
A newspaper headline that runs along the top of a page.
senses.example: The newspaper's streamer announced the election results across the top of page one.

senses.definition: A data storage system, mainly used to produce backups, in which large quantities of data are transferred to a continuously moving tape; a tape drive.
senses.example: The lab's streamer drive backed up the entire server's data every night.

senses.definition: Any mechanism for streaming data.
senses.example: Our engineers built a streamer that pushes sensor readings to the dashboard in real time.

senses.definition: A subscription service that streams content to an audience.
senses.example: My family cancelled our streamer after the price rose again last month.

senses.definition: A person who streams activities on their computer (especially video gaming) to a live online audience.
senses.example: Most streamers are on Twitch

senses.definition: In fly fishing, a variety of wet fly designed to mimic a minnow.
senses.example: The guide tied a streamer on his leader, hoping the trout would strike it.

senses.definition: One who searches for stream tin.
senses.example: The old prospector was a streamer, panning gravel along the creek for tin.

senses.definition: A stream or column of light shooting upward from the horizon, constituting one of the forms of the aurora borealis.
senses.example: Green streamers of the aurora shimmered above the frozen lake all night.

core.definition: A long, narrow strip of paper, fabric, or ribbon used as festive decoration, often thrown or hung at parties.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STREE, and the final -er is a reduced, r-colored vowel, so the word ends softly rather than with a full 'air' sound. Keep the r clear after the initial consonants.

nuance.connotation: Positive and festive. Streamers suggest celebration, parties, parades, and sports wins.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hang or toss streamers at birthday parties, weddings, sports events, and parades, often with balloons. In journalism, a streamer is a headline that runs across the top of a page. Note that many Americans now associate streamer with someone who broadcasts live video online, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A banner is a larger, often printed sign or headline. A streamer is thin, flexible, and often paper or plastic.
Ribbon is usually satin or fabric used for gift wrapping or sewing. Streamers are usually paper or plastic and made for decoration.
Confetti is small bits of paper scattered. Streamers are long strips that are hung or tossed as one piece.

examples.everyday: Can you help me hang the streamers before the guests arrive?
examples.professional: Marketing wants paper streamers at the booth for the product launch, so please order them with the banners.
examples.analytical: The streamers in the parade become, in the essay, a symbol of public joy that fades quickly once the crowd goes home.

nuance.analogy: A streamer is like a kite's tail, a bright line that trails behind motion and shows the direction of movement.
nuance.etymology: From stream (Middle English streme, from Old English strēam) with the agent or object ending -er.
common_mistakes: Using streamer for confetti; confetti is small pieces, while streamers are long strips.
Missing the newer meaning of streamer for a live online broadcaster in tech and gaming contexts.

senses.definition: On a weather chart, a line that is tangent to the flow of the wind.
senses.example: The meteorologist drew each streamline tangent to the wind on the surface chart.

senses.definition: A line that is tangent to the velocity of flow of a fluid; equivalent to the path of a specific particle in that flow.
senses.example: Engineers plotted the streamline through the nozzle to track a particle's path.

senses.definition: To design and construct the contours of a vehicle etc. so as to offer the least resistance to its flow through a fluid.
senses.example: The automaker streamlined the new sedan's body to cut wind resistance.

senses.definition: To simplify or organize a process in order to increase its efficiency.
To modernize.
senses.example: The city plans to streamline the permit process for small business owners.

core.definition: To simplify a process or organization by removing unnecessary steps so that it works more efficiently.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and the 'ai' is a clear diphthong, as in 'line'. Learners sometimes add a vowel between 'm' and 'l', so say it as one smooth syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests improvement, although it can sound like a cover for layoffs in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'streamline' in business meetings and reports to mean making a process simpler and faster. It is a standard management term, and it is also used for product design. In casual speech, people say 'make it simpler' or 'cut the extra steps'. Be careful, since some employees hear it as code for cuts.

distinctions.note: Simplify means make less complicated, while streamline focuses on making a process or flow more efficient.
Optimize suggests finding the best possible result, while streamline means removing obstacles and steps.

examples.everyday: We're trying to streamline our morning routine so we're not rushing out the door.
examples.professional: Let's streamline the approval process so that marketing doesn't wait a week for every sign-off.
examples.analytical: The reform aimed to streamline bureaucracy, but critics argue that removing checkpoints can weaken accountability.

nuance.analogy: Like smoothing a bumpy road so the car can travel faster with less friction.
nuance.etymology: From stream and line, originally a technical term for a smooth, flow-following shape in engineering.
common_mistakes: Using 'streamline' only for vehicles, when it is widely used for processes and organizations.
Writing 'streamline up' or 'streamline out' instead of simply 'streamline the process'.

conversation.text: We need to streamline the approval process; it takes too long.
The new tool streamlined our reporting.
Let's streamline the onboarding steps for new customers.

senses.definition: In a strenuous manner.

core.definition: With great effort, energy or determination, often in a way that is tiring or intense.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle part is 'yoo' with a glide, and the final syllable is a light 'lee'. Many learners stress the second syllable or drop the y sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It emphasizes effort and determination, sometimes with an edge of seriousness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use strenuously in formal writing, news and debate, such as 'strenuously deny' or 'strenuously object'. In casual talk, people typically say 'really hard' or 'totally' instead. The word often pairs with verbs of denial or objection, and it sounds stiff in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Vigorously stresses energy and forcefulness; strenuously adds a sense of hard effort against difficulty or resistance.
Intensely describes depth of feeling or concentration; strenuously describes physically or mentally taxing effort.

examples.everyday: My brother strenuously insisted that he did not eat the last slice of pie.
examples.professional: Our legal team strenuously objected to the new contract terms during the review meeting.
examples.analytical: Early reformers strenuously argued that scripture alone should govern the church's teaching.

nuance.analogy: Strenuously is like pushing a heavy cart uphill with every muscle: the effort is visible and hard-earned.
nuance.etymology: From strenuous, from Latin strenuus, meaning vigorous or brisk, plus -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'strenuously' for physical activity in casual talk: say 'worked really hard' rather than 'worked strenuously'.
Misplacing the stress as STREN-yoo-us-LEE or dropping the y sound in the middle syllable.

senses.definition: To partly obliterate text by drawing a continuous line through the center thereof, usually to indicate the deletion of an error or obsolete information.
senses.example: It is useful to strike through an incorrect text, leaving it legible, to demonstrate that it is an incorrect usage.

core.definition: To draw a line through text to show that it is deleted or no longer valid.

pronunciation.tip: Through carries the main stress here, and the gh is silent, so the word is pronounced throo. Keep the r clear and the k in strike crisp.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a practical editing term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use strike through in editing, proofreading, legal drafts and word processors to show deleted or outdated text while keeping it visible. In handwritten notes, people more often say cross out. A natural reply in a meeting is simply Got it, or a question about which version to use.

distinctions.note: Delete removes text entirely, while strike through keeps it visible so readers can see the change.
Cross out is the everyday term for handwriting, while strike through is the standard term for documents and digital editing.

examples.everyday: I struck through the wrong phone number on the list and wrote the new one beside it.
examples.professional: Please strike through the old deadline in the draft and add the new one in bold.
examples.analytical: A strike-through preserves the original wording, so later readers can see exactly what the author revised and why.

nuance.analogy: Striking through text is like crossing out a line on a grocery list: you can still read it, and you know it no longer applies.
nuance.etymology: Strike from Old English strīcan plus through from Old English thurh, meaning from one side to the other.
common_mistakes: Using strike through as a noun; the noun is strikethrough, and the verb is strike through.
Saying strike through the paper when you mean delete the paper; the phrase refers to text, not to the whole page.

senses.definition: An act of hitting; a blow, a hit.
senses.example: a stroke on the chin

senses.definition: An act of striking with a weapon; a blow.
senses.example: Singapore plans to cane scammers and scam mules, with mandatory caning of at least six strokes for scammers and discretionary caning for mules.

senses.definition: A single movement with a tool; also, an impact of a tool on an object.
The hitting of a bell or similar by the clapper or hammer of a clock; the sound thereof; the time when this occurs.
senses.example: on the stroke of midnight

senses.definition: An act of hitting or trying to hit a ball; also, the manner in which this is done.
senses.example: Every stroke he made on the course was smooth and controlled, even under pressure.

senses.definition: A single act of striking at the ball with a club; also, at matchplay, a shot deducted from a player's score at a hole as a result of a handicapping system.
senses.example: At match play, he got a stroke on the difficult sixteenth hole because of his handicap.

senses.definition: A point awarded to a player in case of interference or obstruction by the opponent.
senses.example: The referee awarded him a stroke after his opponent blocked the shot deliberately.

senses.definition: The hitting of a ball with a racket; also, the movement of the racket and arm that produces that impact.
senses.example: Her forehand stroke was fast, and the ball skimmed the net before landing.

senses.definition: A movement similar to that of hitting.
senses.example: the stroke of a bird’s wing in flying

senses.definition: One of a series of beats or movements against a resisting medium, by means of which movement through or upon it is accomplished.
senses.example: the stroke of a bird’s wing in flying

senses.definition: The movement of an oar or paddle through water: either the cycle of movement as a whole, or the propelling phase (as opposed to the return); the manner in which such movements are made; a rowing style.
senses.example: The coach corrected the rowers' stroke, urging a longer, smoother pull through the water.

senses.definition: The rower nearest the stern of the boat, the movement of whose oar sets the rhythm for the other rowers; the position in the boat occupied by this rower.
senses.example: The coxswain asked Mia to take stroke, setting the pace for the whole crew.

senses.definition: A movement of the arms and legs which propels a swimmer through the water; a specific combination of such movements, constituting a swimming style.
senses.example: butterfly stroke

senses.definition: A beat or throb, as of the heart or pulse.
senses.example: I felt each stroke of my pulse as I waited for the test results.

senses.definition: A single movement or thrust of a reciprocating device (such as a piston or connecting rod).
senses.example: For the pistons of a four-stroke engine, the exhaust stroke follows the power stroke.

senses.definition: The length of this movement.
senses.example: The bore times the stroke times the number of cylinders equals displacement.

senses.definition: A thrust of the penis during sexual intercourse.
An act causing hurt or death, especially when seen as divine punishment.
senses.example: the stroke of death

senses.definition: A damaging occurrence, especially if sudden; a blow, a calamity.
senses.example: The sudden loss of his job was a cruel stroke of bad luck.

senses.definition: An amount of work; specifically, a large amount of business or work.
senses.example: a stroke of business

senses.definition: A powerful or sudden effort by which something is done or produced; also, something accomplished by such an effort; an achievement, a feat.
senses.example: a stroke of genius

senses.definition: A single movement of a paintbrush, chisel, pen, pencil, or similar implement; a line or mark made by such an implement.
senses.example: With a single bold stroke, she painted the sky a deep, stormy blue.

senses.definition: A line making up a written character.
senses.example: Each stroke of the Chinese character must be written in the correct order.

senses.definition: In Unicode: the formal name of the individual horizontal strikethroughs (as in "A̶").
senses.example: The Unicode stroke U+0336 combines with a letter to produce a strikethrough effect.

senses.definition: A distinctive expression in a written composition; a touch.
senses.example: to give some finishing strokes to an essay

senses.definition: Backstage influence.
senses.example: Her uncle had enough stroke at the paper to get her article published quickly.

senses.definition: A masterful or effective action.
senses.example: Her closing argument was a stroke of genius that won over the jury.

senses.definition: An individual discharge of lightning, particularly if causing damage.
senses.example: A flash of lightning may be made up of several strokes. If they are separated by enough time for the eye to distinguish them, the lightning will appear to flicker.

senses.definition: An individual social interaction whereby one gives another attention or recognition.
senses.example: A friendly stroke from the manager made the new hire feel welcome.

senses.definition: The effect or result of a striking; affliction or injury; a bruise or wound; soreness.
senses.example: The stroke of the hammer left a sore, purple welt on her thumb.

senses.definition: Chiefly in to have a good stroke: appetite.
An act of moving one's hand or an object along a surface in one direction, touching it lightly; a caress.
senses.example: She gave the cat a stroke.

senses.definition: A gesture of assurance given as encouragement; specifically in transactional analysis: a (generally positive) reaction expressed to a person which fulfils their desires or needs.
A flattering or friendly act, comment, etc. done or made to a person to influence them.
The action of hitting the ball with the bat; a shot.
A sudden interruption of blood supply to the brain, causing minor to major brain damage and possible death; it may be either hemorrhagic or thrombotic.
senses.example: suffer a stroke

senses.definition: A sudden attack of any illness, especially if causing loss of consciousness or movement, or when fatal.
senses.example: a stroke of apoplexy

senses.definition: A bow or pluck of a string or strings of a stringed instrument; also, the manner in which a musical instrument is played; hence, a melody, a tune.
To draw the horizontal line across the upright part (of the letter t).
Followed by out or through: to draw a line or lines through (text) to indicate that it is deleted; to cancel, to strike or strike out.
To hit or kick (the ball) with a flowing or smooth motion; also, to score (a goal, a point, etc.) by doing so.
Of a rower or a crew: to row at (a rate of a certain number of strokes (“movements of the oar through water”) per minute).
To act as the stroke (“rower who is nearest the stern of the boat, the movement of whose oar sets the rowing rhythm for the other rowers”) of (a boat or its crew).
senses.example: to stroke a boat

senses.definition: To strike (the water) with one's arms and legs when swimming.
To lengthen the stroke of (an engine) by installing a crankshaft with longer throws.
senses.example: Yes, it's 'only' a small block, but it’s got some tricks up its sleeve — it's been bored, stroked, ported, polished, and fuel-injected.

senses.definition: To swim by making co-ordinated movements with the arms and legs.
To move one's hand or an object (such as a broom or brush) along (a surface) in one direction, touching it lightly; to caress. To masturbate.
To bring (something) to a certain condition by stroking (sense 1).
To give assurance to (someone) through encouragement.
To influence (someone) by convincing or flattering them.
To milk (a cow or other animal); especially, to squeeze the teat of (a cow, etc.) to extract the last bit of milk from the udder; to strap, to strip.
To give a finely fluted surface to (stone) by carving it with a tool.
To sharpen (a knife or other cutting instrument) by honing or rubbing it against a surface.
To soothe (someone); also, to flatter or indulge (someone).
Chiefly followed by out: to suffer loss of brain function when the blood supply to the brain is suddenly interrupted; to have a stroke (noun sense 4).
(rare, poetic) Of a bell or clock: to chime or sound to indicate (the hour, the time, etc.).
senses.label: rare, poetic

senses.definition: (rare) To mark (something) with lines or stripes; to stripe.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (uncommon) To masturbate.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: A single movement made with the arm, a tool, a bat, or a pen, such as a swimming stroke or a golf swing.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable, with a long 'oh' vowel that glides into 'k'. Avoid adding a vowel between 'st' and 'r'; in American speech the 'r' is strong and the 't' is aspirated.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive word for physical movements, but the medical sense (a stroke in the brain) carries serious negative weight.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, 'stroke' is used for movements in swimming, golf, tennis, and painting, as in 'a smooth backstroke' or 'a bold brushstroke.' Be aware that 'stroke' also means a brain attack, which Americans discuss often when talking about health; context usually makes the meaning clear. A natural remark is 'Her backstroke is so smooth,' and a reply might be 'She's been swimming since she was a kid.'

distinctions.note: 'Hit' is a general word for striking something, while 'stroke' suggests a controlled, smooth movement, often with an instrument or limb.
A 'blow' is a forceful strike that may cause harm, while a 'stroke' is usually a gentler or more deliberate movement.

examples.everyday: Her backstroke is so smooth that she barely seems to move in the pool.
examples.professional: The technician checks each stroke of the cutting tool against the spec sheet before approving the batch.
examples.analytical: Each brushstroke in the painting is deliberate, and critics read the stroke as evidence of the artist's hand.

nuance.analogy: A stroke is like a single pass of a pen across paper, one movement that leaves a visible mark.
nuance.etymology: From Old English strācian, to stroke or caress.
common_mistakes: Confusing the everyday movement sense with the medical sense when a friend says 'had a stroke,' which means a serious illness.
Using 'stroke' for a single hit in a fight; for that, 'blow' or 'hit' is more natural.

stroke.etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English *strok*, *stroke* (“blow from a weapon, cut”), from Old English *strāc*, from **straik*, from Proto-Germanic **straikaz* (“stroke”), from Proto-Indo-European **streyg-* (“to rub, stroke; to shear; to strike”).

senses.definition: The property of being suave.

core.definition: The quality of being smooth, polished and easily charming in manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with the 'ah' vowel of 'cot'. The final syllable is a weak, reduced 'nus', not a strong 'nes'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, though it can carry a hint that the polish is a bit too practiced or slick.
nuance.usage_note: Suaveness is rare in everyday American talk; people more often say smoothness, polish or charm. It appears in reviews and writing about actors, politicians and hosts. Americans sometimes use it with a slight edge, implying the polish is calculated. A natural reply is 'Yeah, he definitely has that polish.'

distinctions.note: Suaveness and suavity mean nearly the same thing; suavity is more common in formal writing, while suaveness is less frequent.
Charm is warmth that draws people in; suaveness is polish and ease, often more self-assured and sometimes slick.

examples.professional: Her suaveness with clients helps us close deals, but the team still needs clearer written follow-up.
examples.analytical: The character's suaveness is a mask, and the novel uses his polished manners to expose the cruelty beneath.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-oiled door: nothing sticks and nothing squeaks, so you hardly notice it working.
nuance.etymology: From suave plus -ness, from French suave, from Latin suavis.
common_mistakes: Using suaveness for politeness in general; it implies polish and social ease.
Pronouncing the first vowel as 'ay' instead of the American 'ah'.

senses.definition: Without signs and symptoms that are detectable by physical examination or laboratory test; not clinically manifest.
senses.example: Some conditions may remain subclinical until they resolve without intervention, whereas others worsen from subclinical to clinical status.

senses.definition: Where some criteria are met but not enough to reach the status of a clinical diagnosis.
senses.example: The patients had subclinical symptoms that never met the threshold for a formal diagnosis.

senses.definition: Less than is needed for clinical reasons.
senses.example: Off-label use of certain drugs at subclinical dosages has been a theme in realms of activity such as metabolic optimization, weight loss, body hacking, and neurohacking (e.g., nootropics); such drugs include metformin, beta-blockers, and others.

core.definition: Showing signs of a disease that are too mild to be diagnosed by standard clinical examination or tests.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on KLIN, not on SUB; the same root appears in 'clinic' and 'clinical'. Reduce the last two syllables to schwa-like sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, though for patients it can suggest a condition that needs watching.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors and researchers use this word to describe conditions that are present but do not yet meet the threshold for a clinical diagnosis. Patients often hear it in conversations about lab results, such as slightly elevated thyroid levels. Outside medicine, Americans would say 'mild' or 'not yet serious'.

distinctions.note: Asymptomatic means having no symptoms, while subclinical often refers to abnormal test results or signs that are not yet a full clinical diagnosis.

Preclinical refers to a stage before disease can be assessed in patients, often in research or animal studies, while subclinical describes a condition present in a patient but below the diagnostic threshold.

examples.everyday: My doctor said my thyroid is only slightly off, a subclinical issue, so she wants to recheck it in six months.
examples.professional: The model flags subclinical cases in patient records, so we need labeled data that captures early signs.
examples.analytical: The line between subclinical and clinical disease depends on diagnostic thresholds that medical communities revise over time.

nuance.analogy: Like a smoke detector that senses smoke before flames appear: the problem exists, but it is not yet obvious.
nuance.etymology: From sub- 'under' plus clinical, from Greek klinikos 'of a bed', from klinē 'bed'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in SUB-clin-ik-al.
Using 'subclinical' to mean 'minor' in everyday talk, when it specifically means below the diagnostic threshold.

senses.definition: The achievement of one's aim or goal.
senses.example: His third attempt to pass the entrance exam was a success.

senses.definition: Financial profitability.
senses.example: Don't let success go to your head.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, achieves assumed goals.
senses.example: Scholastically, he was a success.

senses.definition: The fact of getting or achieving wealth, respect, or fame.
senses.example: She is country music's most recent success.

core.definition: The achievement of something you wanted or aimed for; a good result, or the state of having achieved a goal.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SES, and the first syllable is a weak uh sound. The s sounds are both hard, so do not change the second s into a z.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Success is one of the most approving words in American English, though it can be used with a slightly sarcastic tone (as in 'Oh, great success!').
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'success' in almost every setting, from job interviews to birthday toasts ('Congratulations on your success!'). A common reply to 'Did it work?' is 'Yes, it was a success!' The word can also mean making money, as in 'business success'. Someone who has done well is often called 'a success story'.

distinctions.note: Achievement often refers to a specific accomplishment through effort, while success is broader and includes the overall outcome or status.
Win means defeating someone or getting a prize, while success can happen without any competition.
Luck is what happens by chance; success suggests that effort, skill, or planning contributed to the result.

examples.everyday: The cookies were a huge success at the party, and everyone asked for the recipe.
examples.professional: The success of the pilot program depends on how quickly we can onboard the new users.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguishes true success in living well from mere wealth or reputation.

nuance.analogy: Success is like the finish line of a race: the goal you were running toward, reached after the effort.
nuance.etymology: From Latin successus, from succedere (to go up under, come after, succeed).
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun success with the verb succeed or adjective successful.
Saying 'success to do' instead of 'success in doing'.
Using 'a success' for a person who did well without making clear whether you mean a thing or person who succeeded.

senses.definition: Containing no refined sugar as an ingredient.

core.definition: Made without sugar, especially without refined sugar as an ingredient.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SHOOG. The '-less' ending is a reduced 'lus', not a clear 'less' with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sugarless' on product labels or in talk about snacks, gum, or recipes. 'Sugar-free' is more common in grocery stores and carries a specific legal meaning on packaging. In everyday conversation, 'no sugar' or 'sugar-free' is often more natural.

distinctions.note: 'Sugar-free' is the standard label term and has a regulated meaning in the US; 'sugarless' is a looser everyday word.
'Unsweetened' means no sweetener at all, while 'sugarless' may still contain sugar substitutes.

examples.everyday: Could you grab some sugarless gum when you're at the checkout?
examples.professional: The new snack line is sugarless, so the packaging has to follow the current FDA rules for making that claim.
examples.analytical: A sugarless diet is not automatically healthy, because the substitutes and processed alternatives used to replace sugar also deserve careful examination.

nuance.analogy: Sugarless food is like a house without a particular piece of furniture: it still works, but the taste is different from what you expected.
common_mistakes: Using 'sugarless' on labels where 'sugar-free' is the expected legal term.
Pronouncing the final syllable 'less' with a clear e instead of the reduced 'lus'.

senses.definition: Of food, drink, etc. containing or covered with a large amount of sugar.
senses.example: The sugary glaze on the donuts made my teeth ache just looking at them.

senses.definition: Exaggeratedly sweet and pleasant, often to the point of aversion.
senses.example: The greeting card's sugary verses about eternal love made me cringe.

senses.definition: (dated) Fond of sweets.
senses.example: Grandma was a sugary old soul who never met a candy she didn't love.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: A place where maple-juice is manufactured.
senses.example: In early spring, we visited a sugary in Vermont to watch the maple sap being boiled down.

senses.definition: A place where sugar is manufactured.
senses.example: The old sugary on the riverbank closed in the 1990s, leaving hundreds of workers jobless.

core.definition: Containing or covered with a lot of sugar, or exaggeratedly sweet in a way that can become unpleasant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SHOOG. The middle syllable reduces to uh, and the final 'y' is a long ee. Do not pronounce the middle 'ar' as a clear vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sugary' to describe foods like candy, soda, or cereal, and as a criticism of a tone that seems overly sweet or fake. When used for taste, it is neutral; when used for manner, it is usually negative. The noun sense about maple sap or sugar factories is technical and rare in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: 'Sweet' is the neutral general word; 'sugary' implies a stronger or excessive sweetness, often with a negative judgment.
'Sugared' describes food that has sugar added or coated on it; 'sugary' describes how strongly sweet something tastes or sounds.

examples.everyday: That cereal is too sugary for breakfast, so I switched to plain oats.
examples.professional: The sugary tone of the proposal made people question its substance until the data appeared in the appendix.
examples.analytical: A sugary sermon can feel comforting, yet it often avoids the moral seriousness that the gospel requires of its hearers.

nuance.analogy: A sugary tone is like a candle with too much perfume: the pleasant smell becomes overwhelming and makes you want fresh air.
common_mistakes: Using 'sugary' as a neutral word for 'sweet' when speakers usually mean too sweet.
Mispronouncing the middle vowel with a full 'ar' sound instead of a reduced uh.

senses.definition: Any compound of sulfur and a metal or other electropositive element or group.
(organosulfide) A class of organic compounds RSR', where R and R' represent an alkyl group or other organic substituent.
senses.example: The organic chemist reported that the new sulfide dissolved quickly in ethanol solvent.

core.definition: A compound of sulfur with a metal or another element, containing sulfur in the -2 oxidation state, such as hydrogen sulfide or iron sulfide.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the second syllable short and light; the final sound rhymes with 'hide.' Many learners stress the last syllable, saying sul-FIDE, which is wrong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a scientific term, though hydrogen sulfide is associated with a foul, rotten-egg smell.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say sulfide, with the same spelling as the British sulphide. You will hear it in chemistry, geology, mining, and water treatment, and sometimes in everyday talk about a rotten-egg smell in well water, which is usually hydrogen sulfide. Organosulfide, a related term, refers to organic compounds with sulfur bonded to carbon, as in garlic oils.

distinctions.note: A sulfide has sulfur with no oxygen bonded to the metal, while a sulfate has sulfur bonded to four oxygen atoms.
A sulfite is a salt of sulfurous acid with oxygen, whereas a sulfide has no oxygen; sulfites are also used as food preservatives.

examples.everyday: The plumber said the rotten-egg smell in our well water comes from hydrogen sulfide.
examples.professional: The mine tailings have high concentrations of metal sulfides, so we need a containment plan.
examples.analytical: Organosulfide compounds in garlic help explain its distinctive chemistry and smell.

nuance.analogy: Think of a sulfide as sulfur's version of a salt, where the sulfur plays the role of the acid partner but without any oxygen.
